newsitem.title: USA: Republican say Clinton "abused power" in Travelgate.
newsitem.headline: Republican say Clinton "abused power" in Travelgate.

text.p: A Republican congressional report made public on Wednesday charged that President Bill Clinton had abused his power and obstructed investigations into the 1993 firings of staff members from the White House travel office.

The House Government Reform and Oversight Committee issued the 21 pages of excerpts from a more detailed report to be made public later amid partisan squabbling which had characterised much of its two-year investigation.
The report contained no startling revelations about the firings of seven staffers in the office which arranges travel for the press on presidential trips.

Before walking out on a vote to adopt the report, Democrats called it a "partisan smear" and a "multimillion dollar witchhunt" -- language reminiscent of that used when the Senate Whitewater report was issued earlier this year.
Clinton's special associate counsel Mark Fabiani called it "an election-year stunt."

In one of a series of findings on the so-called "Travelgate" affair, the report said: "President Clinton has engaged in an unprecedented misuse of the executive power, abuse of executive privilege and obstruction of numerous investigations into the travel office."

It said the firings had occurred at the instigation of Clinton friend and television producer Harry Thomason, who spread rumours of wrongdoing and who stood to gain by taking over the travel business. But it said the White House "engaged in a conspiracy of silence" about the real reasons, "for damage control purposes."
Hillary Rodham Clinton, "acting on Thomason's baseless allegations of wrongdoing ... asserted (sic) pressure on senior White House staff to fire the travel office employees," the report said.

It said the review minimised Mrs. Clinton's role in the firings. The first lady has denied in sworn statements that she had a role in the firings. Her actions are being examined by Independent Counsel Kenneth Starr.
A memo written by former White House aide David Watkins said he fired the staffers at Mrs. Clinton's insistence.
The head of the office, Billy Dale, was acquitted after being indicted on charges of embezzling money from the office.

An internal White House review into the firings "omitted incriminating information about the president, Mrs. Clinton and Harry Thomason," the report said. "The White House chose to cover up incriminating information for political expediency."
The internal review reprimanded people who were only following orders, the report said.

"It was apparently unthinkable for President Clinton to hold those actually responsible for the firings publicly accountable," it said. "This set in motion a coverup that grew more convoluted with each subsequent investigation."
